taxonomy.label: processes
taxonomy.description: Fundamental carrier-flow capabilities the tool can represent, defined by their mathematical role rather than by named technologies. `Carriers` are the energy or non-energy commodities that flow between processes (e.g. electricity, heat, hydrogen, CO2, water, materials). Only physical processes are in scope; decision-making agents are `actors`.

members.label: boundary exchange
members.description: Carriers can enter or leave the system across its boundary at a defined cost and availability (e.g. fuel supply, primary resource extraction, imports/exports to unmodelled regions).

members.label: one to one
members.description: A single in-flowing carrier can be converted to a single out-flowing carrier (e.g. power plants, electrolysers without heat recovery).

members.label: multi carrier io
members.description: A single conversion process can have several in-flowing and/or out-flowing carriers, each balanced individually, with fixed ratios between them (e.g. back-pressure CHP, fixed heat-recovery fractions).

members.label: flexible ratio
members.description: The ratio between a conversion process's flows can be a decision variable, freely allocated or constrained within a feasible operating region (e.g. heat pumps serving heat and cooling, extraction-condensing CHP).

members.label: temporal transfer
members.description: Carriers can be moved in time (e.g. storage, demand shifting), linking system states across timesteps.

members.label: spatial transfer
members.description: Carriers can be moved between regions as continuous flow subject to transfer-capacity limits, without network physics. See `network.power_flow` / `network.hydraulic_flow` for network physics features.

members.label: delayed transfer
members.description: Carriers can flow continuously in space with a time delay between injection and withdrawal (e.g., river flows, district-heating transit).

members.label: buffered transfer
members.description: Carriers can flow in space with an endogenous in-transit inventory, enabling the flow to accumulate in time (e.g. pipeline linepack).

members.label: discrete transport
members.description: Carriers can be moved in space or exchanged across the system boundary in discrete packets with loading/unloading decisions (e.g. shipping, trucking, rail).

members.label: state changing transfer
members.description: A carrier's physical state can be tracked or converted en route during carrier movement (e.g. gas pressure levels with compressors, heat-network temperature levels).

members.label: inelastic
members.description: A fixed quantity of a carrier can be consumed by a process whose in-flow is balanced like any other process flow. The process can therefore be parameterised and constrained (e.g., to shift consumption in space and time to reflect demand-side management).

members.label: price responsive
members.description: The consumed quantity can be decided in the optimisation against price / willingness-to-pay, via demand bids or stepwise/linear demand curves.

members.label: mobile storage
members.description: A consuming process can have embedded storage whose network attachment and availability vary in space and time, according to user-defined patterns.

groups.label: conversion
groups.description: Carriers can be transformed into other carriers within the system boundary (e.g. power plants, electrolysers, heat pumps, CO2 capture). This enables coupled multi-carrier optimisation.

groups.label: explicit demand
groups.description: Carriers can be consumed within the system boundary by explicit processes with their own balances and constraints, rather than by a fixed exogenous profile parameter.

taxonomy.label: network
taxonomy.description: Network physics can be represented beyond the `processes.spatial_transfer` baseline, where flows are coupled by the physics of the transporting medium rather than by capacity limits alone.

members.label: dc opf
members.description: DC optimal power flow can be modelled.

members.label: ac opf
members.description: Linearised AC optimal power flow can be modelled.

members.label: ptdf
members.description: Power Transfer Distribution Factor <PTDF> limits can be applied, describing the sensitivity of a branch flow to a nodal injection.

members.label: outage factors
members.description: Line/Branch Outage Distribution Factor <LODF/BODF> limits can be applied, describing the sensitivity of a branch flow to the outage of another branch.

members.label: generic constraints
members.description: Generic transmission constraints can be defined by user-supplied sensitivity coefficients not tied to a named physical factor.

members.label: thermal
members.description: Thermal (branch flow magnitude) limits can be applied.

members.label: phase angle
members.description: Phase-angle difference limits between connected buses can be applied.

members.label: transformers
members.description: Shunt and phase-shifting transformers can be represented.

members.label: facts devices
members.description: Flexible AC Transmission System <FACTS> devices can be represented.

members.label: hvdc converters
members.description: Rectifiers, inverters, and HVDC converter stations can be represented.

members.label: unbalanced flows
members.description: Unbalanced flows (asymmetric phases) can be handled in optimal power flow, usually using linearised DistFlow branch equations.

members.label: linearised flow
members.description: Nodal pressure/head can be a decision variable which couples flows using a linearised pressure-drop relationship. Operating limits on that state can be represented in the same formulation (e.g. minimum/maximum nodal pressure, maximum allowable operating pressure <MAOP>, contracted delivery pressure).

members.label: composition tracking
members.description: A single transfer asset can carry a mixture whose constituents are balanced individually, allowing limits on the resulting blend (e.g. hydrogen blend-fraction limits, minimum gross calorific value <GCV>, Wobbe index bounds). Composition-dependent hydraulics (e.g. a density-dependent pressure-drop coefficient) are out of scope.

groups.label: power flow
groups.description: Electrical networks can be represented beyond the `processes.spatial_transfer` baseline.

groups.label: hydraulic flow
groups.description: Pressure-driven networks can be represented for carriers transported through pipes, beyond the `processes.spatial_transfer` baseline (e.g. methane, hydrogen, CO2, district heat/cooling, water).

taxonomy.label: decisions
taxonomy.description: Fidelity of decisions made in the optimisation problem. Approximating a decision's type to keep the problem tractable (e.g. relaxing integer commitment) is `tractability`.

members.label: exogenous capacity
members.description: Asset capacity can be fixed and fully defined in the input data (e.g. for modelling dispatch only).

members.label: continuous capacity
members.description: Asset capacity can be fully endogenous and modelled as a continuous (linear) decision variable. An optional maximum capacity can be specified in the input data (e.g. PV capacity that can be installed at any capacity from zero to a maximum defined by land-use constraints).

members.label: integer investment exogenous capacity
members.description: Asset capacity magnitude can be fixed in the input data, with investment modelled as a discrete (i.e., integer) decision variable (e.g. nuclear power plants whose capacity is fixed & indivisible due to external constraints but the decision to invest in this capacity is as-yet undecided).

members.label: integer investment continuous capacity
members.description: Asset capacity magnitude can be endogenous and modelled as a continuous (linear) decision variable, with investment also endogenous and represented by a binary decision variable. An optional maximum capacity can be specified in the input data (e.g. gas turbines that you want to track as individual units and whose capacity is not fixed by the manufacturer).

members.label: retrofit
members.description: Investment in modifications to an existing asset can be made endogenously, with their own build economics, changing the asset's technical parameters or costs rather than adding standalone capacity (e.g. emissions-abatement retrofits such as flue-gas desulphurisation or CO2 capture, efficiency upgrades, fuel-switching conversions).

members.label: multi period
members.description: The capacity decision can be indexed over several investment periods rather than taken once for the whole horizon. These may be endogenous and decided per investment period with perfect foresight or using a limited foresight method (see `orchestration.coupled_models.limited_foresight`).

members.label: unit commitment
members.description: Assets can be committed as units and _then_ economically dispatched. This generally requires assets to be modelled as discrete units which reflect assets 1-to-1.

members.label: maintenance scheduling
members.description: Asset maintenance / outage schedules can be derived endogenously, co-optimised with operation. Exogenously fixed maintenance windows are instead `constraints.scope.temporal.pointwise`. Resource-constrained maintenance limits are instead `constraints.scope.temporal.cumulative`.

groups.label: investment
groups.description: How an asset's capacity can be represented in the model and optimisation problem.

groups.label: operation
groups.description: The resolution at which asset operation can be represented in the model.

taxonomy.label: constraints
taxonomy.description: Limits on asset investment and operating decisions, split by the model dimension a limit engages, its functional form, and some specific use-cases.

members.label: size bounds
members.description: The capacity that can be installed in a period can be bounded above and/or below (e.g. minimum viable project size, maximum deployable capacity at a site).

members.label: discrete increments
members.description: Capacity added in a period can be restricted to discrete increments rather than any continuous amount (e.g. expansion in integer sets of a fixed block size).

members.label: unit purchase
members.description: Investment unit purchase can be limited within investment periods. Usually requires `decisions.investment.integer_investment_...`.

members.label: availability derating
members.description: An asset's flow can be bounded within a timestep by a time-varying fraction of its capacity (e.g. renewables capacity factor profiles, seasonal or ambient de-rating, partial unavailability).

members.label: minimum stable level
members.displayName: temporal > pointwise > operation > minimum stable level
members.description: A committed asset's flow can be bounded below by a minimum stable operating level, so that it either operates at or above that level or is off. Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: forced offline
members.description: An asset can be required to be off in given timesteps (e.g. forced or planned outage windows). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: forced online
members.description: An asset can be required to be on in given timesteps (e.g. must-run units, an exogenously fixed commitment schedule). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: build rate
members.description: The capacity or number of units added can be limited per investment period, either in absolute terms or relative to what has already been built (e.g. supply-chain build-rate limits, technology growth limits).

members.label: retirement
members.description: Capacity can be removed from the system across investment periods, whether on a fixed schedule or as an endogenous decision (e.g. phased retirement, forced decommissioning at end of technical life).

members.label: availability window
members.description: The investment periods in which an asset may be built or retired can be restricted (e.g. lead times, earliest commissioning dates, periods in which no build is permitted).

members.label: ramping
members.description: The change in an asset's flow between consecutive timesteps can be limited in either direction, within its normal operating range.

members.label: start shut trajectory
members.displayName: temporal > sequential > operation > start shut trajectory
members.description: The flow trajectory while an asset is starting up or shutting down can be limited separately from its normal operating range (e.g. run-up / run-down rates, start profiles). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: commitment duration
members.description: The number of consecutive timesteps an asset must or may remain in a commitment state once it enters it can be limited (e.g. minimum up time, minimum down time, maximum up time). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: start consumption
members.description: A carrier in-flow can be required on a change of commitment state, independent of the asset's out-flow in those timesteps (e.g. start-up fuel offtake). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: capacity target
members.description: Accumulated installed capacity can be bounded above or below, counted at nameplate or at a per-asset de-rating / capacity-credit factor (e.g. policy deployment targets, technical/land-use potential, transmission expansion volume limits, planning margins).

members.label: expansion budget
members.description: Accumulated investment spend can be bounded (e.g. a capital budget across a portfolio, a transmission expansion cost limit).

members.label: event count
members.description: The number of distinct periods in which investment occurs can be limited, so that build-out is lumpy rather than spread evenly across the horizon.

members.label: path dependent
members.description: An investment limit's bound can evolve endogenously from investments made in previous periods, rather than being fixed by an input parameter (e.g. a learning curve raising the capacity deployable in later periods). Approximating this by pre-generating vintaged components is instead `model_definition.component_templating`. The same effect expressed as a cost rather than a limit is `cost.scope.temporal.cumulative.investment`.

members.label: flow volume
members.description: Total carrier in-/out-flow can be bounded over a period (e.g. annual throughput limits, hydro/fuel offtake budgets, take-or-pay quantities). Equivalently expressed as a mean capacity factor over that period.

members.label: impact budget
members.description: Cumulative production or consumption of a non-carrier quantity can be bounded over a period (e.g. an annual CO2 cap, a carbon budget spanning the horizon, a pollutant emissions limit, a water abstraction or land-use budget). The quantity is usually user-definable rather than fixed to a named impact.

members.label: event count
members.description: The number of times a discrete event can occur can be limited over a period (e.g. maximum starts per year, maintenance events limited by available spare-parts/crew resources, limits on storage cycling). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: state duration
members.description: The cumulative number of timesteps an asset spends in a given state can be limited over a period (e.g. total operating hours, total hours unavailable for maintenance). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: path dependent
members.description: An operating limit's bound can evolve endogenously from operation in previous timesteps, rather than being fixed by an input parameter (e.g. battery cycling / calendar degradation lowering available capacity, filter fouling lowering efficiency). The same effect expressed as a cost rather than a limit is `cost.scope.temporal.sequential.operation`.

members.label: investment
members.description: Investment optimisation can start from an existing asset stock rather than from an empty (greenfield) system or can define a desired end-state. This allows pre-existing capacities to be represented (initial) and for backcasting system design (end-state).

members.label: operation
members.description: Initial or end-state operational conditions can be set, and the change in those states between periods can be limited (e.g. start or end storage level requirements; a bound on how far a reservoir's end volume may move from one investment period to the next).

members.label: investment
members.description: A single investment limit can span several assets (e.g. a combined capacity target for a technology fleet, land-use competition between candidate assets).

members.label: operation
members.description: A single operating limit can span several assets (e.g. a carbon budget held across all emitting assets, a combined generation limit for a technology).

members.label: dedicated flow routing
members.description: Carrier out-flow from one asset can be reserved as in-flow to a specific subset of other assets, rather than every flow of a carrier being pooled at the node it is balanced on (e.g. fuel stockpiling ahead of conversion, hydropower cascades, CHP internal steam flows).

members.label: investment
members.description: A single investment limit can span several spatial units (e.g. a national deployment target met by assets at many nodes, a minimum share of new capacity built in each zone).

members.label: operation
members.description: A single operating limit can span several spatial units (e.g. a system-wide emissions cap across a nodal network, a regional self-sufficiency requirement relating generation to demand).

members.label: investment
members.description: A linear relationship can link several investment decision variables (e.g. energy-to-power ratio envelopes on storage capacity).

members.label: operation
members.description: A linear relationship can link several operating decision variables, defining a feasible operating envelope (e.g. CHP heat-power operating regions, combined active/reactive power limits).

members.label: investment
members.description: A quadratic relationship can involve an investment decision variable.

members.label: operation
members.description: A quadratic relationship can involve an operating decision variable (e.g. quadratic fuel curves, loss approximations).

members.label: investment
members.description: A non-linear relationship can involve an investment decision variable (e.g. storage head effects, pressurisation energy curves linked to capacity).

members.label: operation
members.description: A non-linear relationship can involve an operating decision variable (e.g., part-load efficiency, line losses).

members.label: soft constraints
members.description: User-defined or built-in constraints can be reformulated as soft constraints without bespoke implementation per constraint. This is usually via a generic slack-variable-plus-penalty mechanism. This is the generic mechanism; built-in economic threshold costs are instead `cost.functional_form.threshold_deviation.investment` / `cost.functional_form.threshold_deviation.operation`, and the reliability-specific case of relaxing the demand balance is `constraints.reliability.unserved_demand`.

members.label: online headroom
members.description: A requirement can be met from spare capability on assets that are already running, bounded by the gap between an asset's flow and its capacity and by how fast that gap can be closed (e.g. spinning reserve, frequency regulation, flexible ramping products, interruptible load). Limiting an asset's rate of change rather than holding capability to deliver it is `constraints.scope.temporal.sequential.operation.ramping`.

members.label: standby capability
members.description: A requirement can be met from assets that are offline but can be started within a defined response time (e.g. non-spinning reserve, standing or replacement reserve, quick-start plant). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: inertia
members.description: A requirement can be held on stored rotational energy synchronised to the system rather than on power headroom, drawn from an asset's inertia constant rather than from its spare capacity (e.g. a minimum system inertia constraint, synchronous condenser provision).

members.label: loss of load
members.displayName: probabilistic reliability limit > loss of load
members.description: A loss-of-load-probability <LOLP> limit can be applied.

members.label: unserved energy
members.description: An expected-energy-not-served <EENS> limit can be applied.

members.label: unserved demand
members.description: Demand can go unserved at a penalty cost (value of lost load <VOLL>), placing a soft constraint on load shedding within the optimisation.

members.label: contingency constrained
members.description: The optimisation can be constrained to remain feasible following the loss of individual components, over an enumerated set of discrete failure states (e.g. N-1 security-constrained optimal power flow, loss of a compressor station or pipeline segment). Post-contingency corrective action can be co-optimised where the tool supports it.

groups.label: scope
groups.description: Which of the model's dimensions a limit engages, grouped by the most pertinent dimension to a given constraint. Some tool constraints may be a combination of scopes, and will be recorded in multiple places accordingly. E.g., a limit that accumulates over time and is summed across a fleet is recorded under `constraints.scope.temporal` *and* `constraints.scope.assets`. Spanning a dimension usually requires `model_definition.dimension_groups` to define the group the limit applies over.

groups.label: functional form
groups.description: The mathematical form of the relationships the tool can impose between decision variables, and hence the problem class handed to the solver. A linear relationship between an input parameter and a single decision variable (e.g. a fixed efficiency applied to a flow, resource availability scaled by capacity) is the baseline; we do not track it explicitly here. Non-linear and quadratic terms in the objective are instead `cost.functional_form.nonlinear` / `objective.quadratic`.

groups.label: reliability
groups.description: Requirements can be imposed within the optimisation against component failure or short-term imbalance, under deterministic inputs. For deterministic capacity reserve margin, see `constraints.scope.temporal.cumulative.investment.capacity_target`. Post-hoc adequacy assessment is `postprocessing.metrics.probabilistic_reliability_assessment`; probabilistic decision methods are `uncertainty`.

taxonomy.label: cost
taxonomy.description: Costs that can be attached to investment and operating decisions, entering the objective as terms. Cost which varies linearly with a decision variable (e.g. EUR/MW capital cost on nameplate capacity, EUR/MWh operating cost on flow) is the baseline; we do not track it explicitly here. The shape the objective itself can take is `objective`.

members.label: investment
members.description: A cost can be incurred on a change in installed capacity between investment periods (e.g. a retirement / decommissioning charge incurred when capacity is removed). Limiting that change rather than costing it is `constraints.scope.temporal.sequential.investment`.

members.label: start up
members.description: A cost can be incurred each time an asset changes from off to on (start-up cost). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: shut down
members.description: A cost can be incurred each time an asset changes from on to off (shut-down cost). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: ramping
members.description: A cost can be incurred in proportion to the magnitude of change in an asset's flow between timesteps (e.g. ramping wear cost).

members.label: start state dependent
members.displayName: temporal > sequential > operation > start state dependent
members.description: The cost of a change in commitment state can vary with how long the asset has been in the state it is leaving, so that starting from a hot, warm, or cold state incurs a different cost. Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: investment
members.description: A capital cost coefficient can fall or rise with cumulative deployment (e.g. an endogenous learning / experience curve). The same effect expressed as a limit rather than a cost is `constraints.scope.temporal.cumulative.investment.path_dependent`.

members.label: operation
members.description: An operating cost coefficient can change with cumulative prior operation (e.g. maintenance or replacement cost rising with accumulated running hours or storage cycles). The same effect expressed as a limit rather than a cost is `constraints.scope.temporal.cumulative.operation.path_dependent`.

members.label: investment
members.description: A single investment cost can span several assets (e.g. a shared site development or grid connection charge incurred once for a group of candidates).

members.label: operation
members.description: A single operating cost can span several assets (e.g. a fleet-level fixed O&M charge, a contract priced on combined output).

members.label: investment
members.description: A single investment cost can span several spatial units (e.g. a corridor reinforcement charge triggered by build-out at any of its nodes).

members.label: operation
members.description: A single operating cost can span several spatial units (e.g. a national levy or carbon price applied across every node at once).

members.label: investment
members.description: Initial capital cost can be incurred on asset purchase, irrespective of capacity (e.g. land purchase, design phase). Usually requires `decisions.investment.integer_investment_...`.

members.label: operation
members.description: Operating cost can be incurred for each timestep an asset is committed, irrespective of its flow in that timestep (e.g. no-load cost, stand-by cost). Costs incurred on a change of commitment state are instead `cost.scope.temporal.sequential.operation`. Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: investment
members.description: Capital cost economies of scale can be represented, where cost per capacity decreases with increasing capacity. In some cases, it is possible to describe this without an explicit piecewise constraint. Instead, it may be approximated by multiple assets of the same class (e.g. "wind turbine") that each have different costs and maximum capacities.

members.label: flow dependent
members.description: Cost per unit of flow can vary with the level of that flow (e.g. incremental heat-rate / fuel-offtake curves, part-load cost penalties).

members.label: bid bands
members.description: Cost can be expressed as price-quantity bands, optionally as increments / decrements around a reference dispatch level (e.g. market offer curves, balancing-market incr/decr offers).

members.label: investment
members.description: Costs can be applied to deviation from a contracted or reference investment level (e.g. rebate for providing firm capacity, penalty for exceeding land-use limits).

members.label: operation
members.description: Costs can be applied to deviation from a contracted or reference operating level (e.g. feed-in tariffs, redispatch cost relative to contracted dispatch).

members.label: discounting
members.description: Overnight capital cost can be spread across an asset's economic life using a discount rate (e.g. weighted average cost of capital <WACC>, inflation, a levelised capital carrying rate, separate debt and equity rates).

members.label: fiscal treatment
members.description: Tax and depreciation arrangements can adjust the annuitised cost (e.g. investment tax credits, declining-balance depreciation schedules, production credits).

groups.label: scope
groups.description: Which of the model's dimensions a cost term engages. Some tool costs may be a combination of scopes, and will be recorded in multiple places accordingly. E.g., a carbon price levied on every emitting asset is recorded under `cost.scope.temporal` *and* `cost.scope.assets`. Spanning a dimension usually requires `model_definition.dimension_groups` to define the group the cost applies over.

groups.label: functional form
groups.description: How a cost can vary with the decision variable it attaches to, beyond the linear baseline.

groups.label: annuitisation
groups.description: An asset's capital investment can be annuitised to account for factors linked to its expected economic life and financing arrangements.

taxonomy.label: model definition
taxonomy.description: How the model's parameter space and dimensions can be shaped, grouped, and reused, independent of any single parameter, constraint, or cost.

members.label: dimension groups
members.description: Dimension members can be tagged into named, potentially overlapping groups independent of the model's built-in structural dimensions (e.g. a "coastal assets" or "2030-vintage" tag spanning multiple asset types/nodes). These can be used for dimension aggregation to achieve tractability (e.g. spatial nodes to zones), for filtering on dimensions when applying constraints (e.g. total capacity across group X; seasonal limits), and for analysis/visualisation (`postprocessing.transformation.aggregation`/`postprocessing.transformation.disaggregation`).

members.label: component templating
members.description: Components can inherit parameterisation from a shared template (e.g. an abstract technology definition), with edits to the template cascading to every inheriting component, rather than requiring per-component data entry. Includes programmatic, model-side generation of components from a template (e.g. auto-cloned vintaged expansion candidates approximating `constraints.scope.temporal.cumulative` relationships).

members.label: configurable dimensions
members.description: The dimensionality of an asset parameter (e.g. efficiency, availability) or cost can be configured by the user, limited to a set of tool-defined dimensions.

members.label: extensible dimensions
members.description: A dimension not natively defined by the tool (e.g. a custom vintage, cohort, or scenario axis) can be introduced by the user. Asset parameters/costs and math variables and constraints can be indexed over this new dimension (usually requires custom math - `math.user_defined_math`).

taxonomy.label: math
taxonomy.description: Access to, and user extension of, the underlying mathematical formulation. What that formulation contains is `decisions` / `constraints` / `cost` / `objective`; this covers only what a user can see of it and add to it.

members.label: formulation transparency
members.description: The tool's mathematical formulation can be accessed and inspected (e.g. as rendered equations or a math specification traceable to the built problem).

members.label: problem file export
members.description: The built optimisation problem can be exported in standard formats (e.g. LP/MPS).

members.label: dual extraction
members.description: The built optimisation problem's constraint duals can be extracted (e.g. to approximate wholesale market prices via `postprocessing.metrics.financial.marginal_price`, or to construct a future cost function via `postprocessing.metrics.financial.water_value`).

members.label: piecewise formulation
members.description: Piecewise constructs are available to express nonlinear relationships (`constraints.functional_form.nonlinear`, `cost.functional_form.nonlinear`) in the math, e.g. using LP chord-line or MIP SOS2 constraints. This is the tool offering the constructs for a user to build with; converting a supplied nonlinear function into segments automatically is instead `tractability.reformulation.nonlinear_handling.function_conversion`.

members.label: user defined math
members.description: Users can define their own constraints on the optimisation problem, applied to existing or new decision variables, and write their own objective expression.

taxonomy.label: interface
taxonomy.description: Available options for users and machines to drive the tool: defining, configuring, and structuring a model (`build`); executing a model run (`run`); interacting with model outputs (`analyse`); plus tool-level execution and solver configuration.

members.label: build
members.description: A model can be defined, configured, and structured via a GUI.

members.label: run
members.description: A model run can be executed via a GUI.

members.label: analyse
members.description: Model outputs can be interacted with via a GUI.

members.label: build
members.description: A model can be built using scripting specific to the tool programming language or another programming language for which an API is provided (e.g. a Python API for a package written in C).

members.label: run
members.description: Runs can be launched and managed programmatically.

members.label: analyse
members.description: Results can be analysed programmatically.

members.label: build
members.description: A model can be built via CLI commands. This is usually used to convert between data formats for a given model definition, but may also be used to redefine a model (e.g. reduce dimensions).

members.label: run
members.description: A model run can be launched and managed via CLI commands.

members.label: analyse
members.description: Reports can be created via CLI commands to enable result analysis.

members.label: remote execution
members.description: Runs can be dispatched to and managed on remote compute (cloud, HPC, hosted service) from the tool.

members.label: solver configuration
members.description: Optimiser parameters can be directly configured, including convergence parameters & warm-starting options.

members.label: analysis templates
members.description: Templates can be used to generate consistent reports or dashboards to consolidate model outputs for dissemination.

members.label: charts
members.description: Input or result data can be plotted (e.g. dispatch stacks, time series, duration curves).

members.label: network maps
members.description: Network topology can be rendered, schematically (auto-layout diagrams) or geographically (coordinate-based maps, exports to geographic formats such as KML/GML).

groups.label: gui
groups.description: The tool can be driven via a graphical user interface.

groups.label: api
groups.description: The tool can be driven via a programmatic interface (e.g. language API, web API).

groups.label: cli
groups.description: The tool can be driven via a command line interface.

groups.label: visualisation
groups.description: Model inputs or outputs can be rendered as visual artefacts by the tool, independent of whether a `gui` is available to interact with them.

taxonomy.label: io
taxonomy.description: Data formats, conventions, and mechanisms for moving model input/output data. Computing new parameters is `preprocessing`.

members.label: input
members.description: Input data can be provided in this format.

members.label: output
members.description: Output data can be written in this format.

members.label: input
members.description: Input data can be provided in this format.

members.label: output
members.description: Output data can be written in this format.

members.label: input
members.description: Input data can be read from a database.

members.label: output
members.description: Output data can be written to a database.

members.label: input
members.description: Input data can be read from remote storage.

members.label: output
members.description: Output data can be written to remote storage.

members.label: input
members.description: Input data can be loaded lazily.

members.label: output
members.description: Output data can be written lazily / streamed rather than held fully in memory.

members.label: input
members.description: Input data following a community-recognised convention or ontology can be accepted.

members.label: output
members.description: Outputs can follow a community-recognised convention or ontology. This is useful for regulatory reporting or frictionless data transfer with a downstream process.

groups.label: plain text
groups.description: Data can be handled in human-readable, diff- and version-control-friendly text formats (e.g. CSV, JSON, YAML).

groups.label: binary
groups.description: Data can be handled in compact / compressible, non-human-readable binary formats (e.g. Excel, NetCDF, HDF5, Parquet).

groups.label: database
groups.description: Data can be handled in databases (relational or otherwise).

groups.label: remote storage
groups.description: Data can be read from / written to remote storage (e.g. object stores, cloud drives).

groups.label: lazy loading
groups.description: Data can be loaded lazily / out-of-core, allowing datasets larger than memory.

groups.label: standardised
groups.description: Data can be accepted or emitted following a community-recognised convention or ontology (e.g. Open Energy Ontology <OEO>, IAMC template, the Energy System Description Language <ESDL>, Common Energy System Model <CESM>, SiennaSchemas), including standardised network-data formats (e.g. PSSE RAW, matpower case files, Common Information Model <CIM>).

taxonomy.label: edge effects
taxonomy.description: Distortive effects of system boundaries and linearising model components can be mitigated against. Flows across the spatial boundary are `processes.boundary_exchange`.

members.label: time operational
members.description: Start- / End-of-horizon operational effects can be mitigated (e.g. storage level wrapping).

members.label: time financial
members.description: Start- / End-of-horizon financial effects can be mitigated (e.g. asset investment annuitisation).

members.label: energy balance
members.description: Energy 'destruction' caused by simultaneous in- & out-flow from a lossy transmission/storage asset can be mitigated.

taxonomy.label: actors
taxonomy.description: Heterogeneous decision-making actors can be represented, deviating from the single, central-planner baseline.

members.label: portfolio
members.description: Agent asset portfolios and associated constraints and cost considerations can be represented (e.g. limited cross-portfolio capital investment, risk appetite).

members.label: distributed objectives
members.description: Per-agent profit maximising / risk minimising objectives can be represented within the larger system-level optimisation (e.g. bidding in day-ahead / intra-day markets, behind-the-meter prosumer decisions)

members.label: equilibrium
members.description: Market equilibrium can be computed across actors with competing objectives (e.g. Cournot-Nash oligopoly or Bertrand competition), via complementarity/MCP/bi-level formulations or a quadratic-markup reformulation of the cost-minimisation objective.

members.label: heuristic markup
members.description: Strategic-behaviour price/offer markups can be applied by heuristic or index-based rules rather than computed equilibrium (e.g. Residual Supply Index <RSI>-driven markups, fixed bid adders).

taxonomy.label: objective
taxonomy.description: The objective function can extend beyond minimisation of a single linear cost term.

members.label: multi objective weighted
members.description: Multiple objective terms can be combined via user-set weights into a single objective. Trade-offs can be explored by manual weight variation.

members.label: multi objective pareto
members.description: Pareto-optimal solution sets can be generated across objectives (e.g. epsilon-constraint, evolutionary methods).

members.label: quadratic
members.description: Quadratic objective terms can be passed natively to the solver (e.g. quadratic generation cost curves, welfare maximisation with linear demand curves). Quadratic terms in constraints rather than the objective are `constraints.functional_form.quadratic`.

members.label: tie breaking
members.description: Degenerate solutions (many distinct solutions sharing the same objective value, within tolerance) can be resolved by a documented rule rather than left to solver arbitrariness (e.g. small penalty coefficients applied to otherwise zero-cost decision variables so that they enter the objective explicitly, or a lexicographic secondary objective).

taxonomy.label: uncertainty
taxonomy.description: The decision problem can be restructured to account for parametric or structural uncertainty.

members.label: two stage stochastic
members.description: Two-stage stochastic optimisation can be performed; used in investment decision making under uncertainty.

members.label: multi stage stochastic
members.description: Multi-stage stochastic optimisation can be performed, in which decisions are revised as uncertainty resolves stage by stage. Primarily used for scheduling seasonal storage (e.g. hydropower water values) under uncertain inflows.

members.label: risk aversion
members.description: Risk measures (e.g. Conditional Value at Risk <CVaR>) can be applied to a stochastic optimisation as chance constraints. This weights tail-end outcomes according to a configurable risk tolerance.

members.label: near optimal
members.description: A near-optimal solution set can be generated by relaxing constraints / objectives in the optimisation problem (e.g., Modelling to Generate Alternatives <MGA>).

members.label: robust optimisation
members.description: Worst-case cost can be minimised over an uncertainty set.

taxonomy.label: tractability
taxonomy.description: The computational cost of building and solving the problem can be reduced, trading exactness for speed.

members.label: temporal
members.description: Temporal resolution can be coarsened while remaining contiguous (e.g. hourly to daily) before the model is built. May apply to within-year timesteps or between-year investment periods.

members.label: spatial
members.description: Bordering spatial units can be merged into contiguous zones (e.g. nodal/bus level to regional/bidding zone level). This usually requires `model_definition.dimension_groups` to define aggregation membership.

members.label: temporal
members.description: A full timeseries can be represented by non-contiguous typical periods (days, weeks, months) or by load duration curves.

members.label: spatial
members.description: Spatial units can be clustered by likeness rather than adjacency (e.g. by resource quality or demand profile), so a zone may be geographically discontiguous. This usually requires `model_definition.dimension_groups` to define aggregation membership.

members.label: assets
members.description: Individually defined assets can be automatically aggregated into asset groups for optimisation. This usually requires `model_definition.dimension_groups` to define aggregation membership.

members.label: scenarios
members.description: An ensemble of scenarios / uncertainty samples can be reduced to a smaller representative set with associated weights (e.g. scenario reduction ahead of `uncertainty.multi_stage_stochastic`).

members.label: spatial
members.description: Network elements can be equivalenced, also called network reduction (e.g. reducing to a single voltage level; Ward, Radial Equivalent Independent <REI>, or Kron-reduced equivalents of an external network).

members.label: assets
members.description: A chain of interconnected assets can be collapsed into a single component with an in/out interface, also called black boxing or lumping. This usually requires `constraints.scope.assets.dedicated_flow_routing` between interconnected components.

members.label: temporal
members.description: Timesteps or investment periods (e.g. a user-selected subset of representative weeks) can be systematically filtered out of the built problem.

members.label: spatial
members.description: Spatial units (e.g. below a voltage level, or outside a study region) can be systematically filtered out of the built problem.

members.label: assets
members.description: Individual or groups of assets (e.g. sharing a node or a carrier) can be systematically filtered out of the built problem.

members.label: scenarios
members.description: Scenarios / uncertainty samples can be systematically filtered out of the built problem.

members.label: temporal
members.description: Inter-temporal features can be linked across non-contiguous aggregated periods (e.g. linking storage levels across typical periods).

members.label: spatial
members.description: Inter-spatial features can be linked across geographically discontiguous aggregated zones (e.g. representing transfer capacity between the disjoint parts of a zone).

members.label: formulation
members.description: The mathematical fidelity of the same physical attribute can differ across the model's scope (e.g. discrete units in some investment periods and aggregated capacity in others; unit commitment over the near-term horizon, continuous economic dispatch beyond).

members.label: temporal
members.description: Temporal resolution can vary across the members of another dimension (e.g. hourly timesteps within a focus region and daily elsewhere; hourly for variable renewables and daily for nuclear).

members.label: spatial
members.description: Spatial resolution can vary across the members of another dimension (e.g. nodal detail in near-term investment periods and zonal detail beyond).

members.label: assets
members.description: Asset resolution can vary across the members of another dimension (e.g. individually resolved assets within a focus region and aggregated groups elsewhere).

members.label: scenarios
members.description: Scenario / uncertainty resolution can vary across the members of another dimension (e.g. an `uncertainty.multi_stage_stochastic` scenario tree that samples more finely in near-term stages than in later ones).

members.label: constraint screening
members.description: Constraints unlikely to bind can be omitted or lazily added.

members.label: linearised unit commitment
members.description: Unit commitment can be approximated with continuous (linearised) commitment variables, avoiding integer decision variables.

members.label: convex relaxation
members.description: A non-convex relationship in the model's own formulation can be approximated by a convex relaxation, retaining solver tractability (e.g. second-order-cone relaxation of AC power flow).

members.label: function conversion
members.description: User-defined arbitrary non-linear functions can be automatically converted into valid model inputs (e.g. piecewise segments) without manual discretisation.

members.label: decomposition
members.description: The problem can be split into coordinated sub-problems solved iteratively or in parallel until convergence (e.g. Benders decomposition; Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming <SDDP> for multi-stage stochastic hydropower scheduling).

members.label: approximation
members.description: The solution algorithm can be reformulated to reach a near-optimal answer within tolerance at reduced cost (e.g. progressive hedging, Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming <SDDP>-style cut selection).

members.label: numeric scaling
members.description: Data can be scaled (e.g. by converting base units) to reduce numeric instability and constraint violations in the downstream solver.

groups.label: dimension reduction
groups.description: The number of members along a dimension of the problem can be reduced automatically, The reduction applies uniformly across all other dimensions; a reduction that differs across other dimensions is `tractability.variable_fidelity.resolution`.

groups.label: variable fidelity
groups.description: The fidelity with which the same attribute/dimension is represented can differ across the model's scope.

groups.label: reformulation
groups.description: Discrete or non-linear formulations can be approximated in ways that preserve (mixed-integer) linear tractability.

taxonomy.label: orchestration
taxonomy.description: Multiple complete runs can be coordinated in series/parallel by tool-managed workflows, where the result emerges from the ensemble or its convergence.

members.label: investment
members.description: Investment decisions can be optimised sequentially per period / set of periods, each made without knowledge / with limited knowledge of later periods. Also known as myopic foresight optimisation.

members.label: operation
members.description: Dispatch decisions can be optimised sequentially per set of timesteps (e.g. days), each made without knowledge / with limited knowledge of later timesteps. Also known as rolling horizon optimisation.

members.label: fidelity sequence
members.description: Model instances representing the same system at different fidelity can be run in sequence, with data passed between instances. E.g., a long-term capacity expansion run with linearised dispatch, passing data to a short-term, unit-commitment dispatch run to stress test the capacities chosen by the lower fidelity long-term run.

members.label: market sequence
members.description: Model instances representing successive market stages can be executed together with bidirectional data exchange (e.g. interleaved day-ahead/real-time runs passing offers and dispatch baselines forward and initial conditions back).

members.label: convergence iteration
members.description: Runs can be repeated, exchanging data each time, until convergence with respect to (often nonlinear) relationships that cannot be represented directly in a single problem (e.g. competitive market simulation, iterating on line reactances, simulation-optimisation loops).

members.label: scenario runs
members.description: Discrete, named scenario ensembles can be executed in batch in series/parallel with collated outputs.

members.label: sampled runs
members.description: Run ensembles can be executed over a sampled uncertainty space (e.g. Monte Carlo), with collated outputs. Used e.g. for post-hoc resource adequacy assessment (`postprocessing.metrics.probabilistic_reliability_assessment`) or portfolio price-risk quantification. Distinct from `scenario_runs` (discrete, named scenarios).

groups.label: coupled models
groups.description: Two or more model runs can be executed together with tool-managed data exchange between them.

taxonomy.label: preprocessing
taxonomy.description: Parameters can be derived from user-defined input data before running the model. Moving/storing data is `io`.

members.label: forecasting
members.description: A user-defined generation / load profile can be automatically scaled or reshaped to meet user-defined forecast targets (e.g. change in annual total or peak).

members.label: resource conversion
members.description: Model profiles can be derived within the tool from primary resource or weather data via physical response models. This may be technology models converting resource to availability or efficiency (e.g. wind speed to turbine capacity factor, temperature to heat pump COP). It may also be weather-response demand functions (e.g. temperature-driven gas or heating demand).

members.label: demand
members.description: Nodal demand can be distributed from an aggregate total.

members.label: network geometry
members.description: Transmission/pipeline line distances or routing can be derived from node coordinates.

members.label: slack
members.description: Slack can be allocated in a distributed manner across nodes.

members.label: download
members.description: Data can be downloaded directly within the tool from an open or proprietary source rather than being specified by the user.

members.label: model catalogue
members.description: Pre-built model datasets/examples can be retrieved from a catalogue as starting points for new models.

members.label: scenario generation
members.description: Scenario ensembles can be generated from user-defined parameters or sampling rules, for execution as `orchestration.scenario_runs` or `orchestration.sampled_runs`.

members.label: input validation
members.description: Input data can be validated against the tool's expected structure and value ranges before a run, with informative failures.

groups.label: spatial distribution
groups.description: A user-defined parameter can be automatically distributed spatially using other spatial parameters.

taxonomy.label: postprocessing
taxonomy.description: Postprocessing analyses that can be triggered by the tool based on model outputs, on a per-asset or system-wide basis.

members.label: emissions
members.description: GHG or other pollutant emissions can be calculated.

members.label: resource use
members.description: Non-carrier resource consumption (e.g. water, land, materials) can be calculated.

members.label: socioeconomic
members.description: Socioeconomic impacts (e.g. job creation) can be calculated.

members.label: curtailment
members.description: Asset generation curtailment can be calculated.

members.label: capacity factor
members.description: Asset generation relative to full-load generation, averaged over the model horizon, can be calculated.

members.label: full load hours
members.description: The number or fraction of timesteps in the model horizon that assets are operating at or close to their full load can be calculated. Distinct from `capacity_factor` as the same average output can arise from very different duty cycles, affecting e.g. asset lifetime.

members.label: levelised cost
members.description: Levelised cost of electricity or other carriers can be calculated.

members.label: net present value
members.description: Net present value of the modelled system or a subset of assets can be calculated.

members.label: asset accounts
members.description: Asset-level revenue / cost accounting can be performed.

members.label: marginal price
members.description: Shadow prices can be extracted via `math.dual_extraction`, used to approximate wholesale market prices or as an input to `price_formation`, `contract_settlement` and soft-constraint interpretation.

members.label: price formation
members.description: Prices can be constructed by a documented market rule rather than taken directly from optimisation duals (e.g. uniform pricing via a relaxed re-solve, uplift / fixed-cost-recovery adders, iterative markup calibration to recover long-run marginal cost, marginal-loss-factor settlement).

members.label: water value
members.description: A future cost function (water value) can be constructed as a reusable, exportable artefact from shadow prices extracted via `math.dual_extraction` (e.g. from Benders / SDDP cuts), forecasting the marginal cost of hydro and other seasonal storage devices for use in shorter-term scheduling under uncertain input parameters.

members.label: contract settlement
members.description: Contracts can be settled post-hoc against realised dispatch and prices, without altering the underlying optimisation (e.g. Contracts-for-Difference <CfD>, Power/energy Purchase Agreements <PPA>, swaps, caps/floors, Financial Transmission Rights <FTR>, Settlement Residue Auctions <SRA>).

members.label: transfer capacity
members.description: Grid transfer capacities between regions or zones can be calculated.

members.label: flow sensitivity
members.description: Flow-sensitivity metrics (e.g. power transfer distribution factors, line outage distribution factors) can be calculated.

members.label: loss of load
members.displayName: probabilistic reliability assessment > loss of load
members.description: Loss of load probability/expectation <LOLP> can be calculated.

members.label: unserved energy
members.description: Expected energy not served <EENS> can be calculated.

members.label: capacity credit
members.description: Effective load carrying capacity <ELCC> can be calculated.

members.label: aggregation
members.description: Outputs can be aggregated across dimensions into broader groups for analysis and dissemination. This usually requires `model_definition.dimension_groups` to define aggregation membership.

members.label: disaggregation
members.description: Outputs can be redistributed back to an initial, pre-`tractability.dimension_reduction` resolution (e.g. so that capacity-expansion results can be handed off to a full-resolution power-flow model).

members.label: scenario comparison
members.description: Outputs of multiple scenario/ensemble runs can be collated and compared.

groups.label: metrics
groups.description: Quantities can be computed from model outputs and reported per-asset or system-wide.

groups.label: transformation
groups.description: Model outputs can be reshaped and collated, without deriving new quantities from them.

taxonomy.label: traceability
taxonomy.description: Information can be traced throughout the modelling pipeline, including for debugging, diagnostics, and transparency.

members.label: run logs
members.description: Run logs can be made available (e.g. in text files), for use in debugging failing model runs.

members.label: infeasibility diagnosis
members.description: Infeasible problems can be diagnosed (e.g. irreducible infeasible subset (IIS) generation, named constraint violations).

members.label: provenance
members.description: Data sources, versions, and licences can be defined for inputs.

members.label: units
members.description: Physical units attached to data can be tracked and validated through the pipeline (to enable e.g., unit-consistency checking, automatic conversion, auto-scaling).

members.label: propagation
members.description: Outputs can be linked back to the inputs and settings used to create them.

members.label: intermediate access
members.description: Intermediate pipeline artefacts (e.g. built problem data, solver state) can be exposed to the user.

groups.label: metadata
groups.description: Metadata can be defined for modelling inputs and outputs.

useCases.name: Bidding Zone Review
useCases.description: Model impact on energy system design, systemwide costs, and / or transmission system congestion of implementing new market mechanisms or updating existing ones. This could include bidding zone reviews; direct subsidies; feed-in-tariffs; contract auctions.
assumptions: The optimization will be run over individual years with myopic foresight over days or weeks within the year.

Available transmission lines are set by scenarios from the network development plan (NDP), are limited between bidding zones using power transfer distribution factors, and are represented using security-constrained AC optimal power flow.
Generator capacities are fixed by the integrated resource plan (IRP).

Assets are resolved individually where possible and their unit commitment as well as economic dispatch is represented with the aim of accurately representing the day-ahead and intra-day markets. This may require iterating between an optimisation and simulation run to resolve bidding decisions.
Only the power system is considered.
The system supply-demand balance is relaxed. Load shedding is limited with constraints on EENS and LOLP applied alongside a value of lost load (VOLL).

Resilience to weather uncertainty is addressed using multi-stage stochastic optimisation applied across rolling horizon windows. This may require decomposing the problem into different optimisation problems that are iterated upon until convergence.
Users require a GUI to navigate model preparation, optimisation, and analysis.

useCases.name: Integrated Resource Planning (IRP)
useCases.description: Create a set of high-level scenarios of e.g. 2050 decarbonised energy system designs for use in guiding policy implementation, creating procurement plans, and providing boundary conditions for investors, utilities, and local authorities to develop their own plans. Future scenarios account for full sector coupling and GHG emission accounting.
assumptions: The optimization will be run with perfect foresight over the full model horizon, which spans multiple years/decades.

Investment decisions may occur once every N (> 1) years.
 Within a year, the timeseries is contiguous but may be resampled.
Large assets (e.g. thermal power plants, hydro) are individually resolved; distributed assets (e.g. wind & solar) are grouped per project or region.
Large assets are represented with unit commitment due to operating constraints which require resolving (ramping, uptimes, run ups. etc.).
Hydro cascading and technology chaining internal to power plants is not represented.
Generator contract arrangements (e.g. min/max dispatch obligations) are represented.
Technology economies of scale and bidding levels are represented.
Hydro storage levels are set by the model at the start/end of the time horizon.
Demand-side flexibility is represented by time-shiftable loads.
LOLP/EENS constraints are not explicitly set; the standard system balance constraint will set this to effectively zero energy not served.
Curtailment rates are calculated in post-processing.
Robustness and MGA techniques will not be employed. Sensitivity analysis will be limited to a small set of tests and therefore not require monte carlo techniques.
There is sufficient computational capacity to run the model with defined spatio-temporal scope and resolution without employing decomposition techniques.
transmission line and storage charge/discharge losses are not defined, so "unphysical" energy destruction does not need to be mitigated against.
User-defined constraints are necessary to represent policy targets (e.g. systemwide limits, possibly only affecting a subset of technologies).
Users require a GUI to navigate model preparation, optimisation, and analysis.
The gas distribution network is resolved alongside the electricity transmission network.
Transmission between regions is represented using DC optimal power flow.

useCases.name: Network Development Plan (NDP) / Transmission Planning Process (TPP)
useCases.description: Create a set of detailed scenarios of e.g., 2050 transmission grid designs for use in guiding policy implementation and providing boundary conditions for investors, utilities, and local authorities to develop their own plans. The transmission plans will be optimized based on high-level scenarios of decarbonised energy system findings.
assumptions: The optimization will be run with perfect foresight over the full model horizon, which spans multiple years/decades.
Generator capacities are fixed by the integrated resource plan (IRP) at each of the model investment years.
Assets are grouped and only their dispatch, not their unit commitment is represented.
Contracted operating arrangements and regulated limits (e.g. on emissions) defined in the IRP are applied.
Non-linear transmission characteristics need to be defined, using piecewise linearisation.
Transmission between zones is represented using AC optimal power flow.
The transmission network is accurately represented, albeit aggregated into larger zones.
Transmission limits are defined by power limits (grid transfer capacities).
There is sufficient computational capacity to run the model with defined spatio-temporal scope and resolution without employing decomposition techniques.
Investment and storage asset horizon edge effects are ignored.
The system supply-demand balance is relaxed. Load shedding is limited with constraints on EENS and LOLP applied alongside a value of lost load (VOLL).
User-defined decision variables may be required to enable one-off transmission system quirks to be suitably constrained.
Users require a GUI to navigate model preparation, optimisation, and analysis.
Different weather and demand years are used to stress-test the model but not as a formal Monte Carlo analysis.
The output data must be formatted appropriately for regulatory approval.

useCases.name: Policy Target Setting
useCases.description: Political exercise to set carbon emission pathways to meet future year targets
assumptions: The optimization will be run with perfect foresight over the full model horizon, which spans multiple decades at 5 year resolution.
Spatial scope is national and single node. Could be multinode at national resolution if multinational but not chosen here.
Year is represented by representative time slices (heuristics: day/night/peak/season). Could also be representative periods based on automated timeseries clustering, but not chosen here.
Storage aggregated. Need mathematical representation to handle inter-slice storage.
Assets are always grouped.
Sub-group assets by their costs/resource (pre-processed). Includes e.g. wind techs, sources of fuels etc. Group assets back up in postprocessing.
User constraints/variables are necessary to limit total emissions etc. for subsets of the system being defined.
No representation of complex asset characteristics.
Flexible demand is necessary.
Endogenous learning (piecewise investment cost) not used as it distorts the model.
Grid-transfer capacities used for multi-node models.
Multi-carrier, including electricity, hydrogen, natural gas, heat, etc.
Demands are end-use services (e.g. "vehicle kms" for transport demands).
Extraction of fossils are represented as assets, competing with e.g. imports.
Sensitivity scenarios will be conducted but detailed sensitivity analysis/stochastic optimisation is beyond the scope of this study.
Outages represented by a reserve margin of dispatchable capacity. Assets also have an availability factor.
GUI is necessary, particularly for outputs.
Marginal/shadow prices required to compare market prices between scenarios.
Technology-specific discount rates are used to represent consumer preferences on payback periods (a.k.a. hurdle rates).
Demand elasticity is represented in loads.

useCases.name: Asset portfolio investment plan
useCases.description: Create an asset portfolio investment plan as a private / public utility company. This plan will be guided by national / regional plans (IRPs, NDPs, etc.), the company's   current risk appetite, and any upcoming changes to market mechanisms / subsidies which may impact revenue.
assumptions: The optimization will be run over individual years both with perfect foresight (capacity planning) and with myopic foresight over days or weeks within the year (operating revenue analysis).
Financial and operational horizon edge effects must be considered as the portfolio includes storage devices.
No timeseries simplification is undertaken because the spatial and generator scope is limited to cover only the assets in the portfolio.
The rest of the system develops according to the scenarios set out by the integrated resource plan (IRP) and network development plan (NDP) and is resolved coarsely.
Portfolio assets are resolved individually with unit commitment characteristics (ramp rate, up/down-time, etc.) and non-linear operating and financial considerations that are piecewise linearised.
Hydro cascading is represented, as well as asset linking within power plants, where those power plants have multiple possible asset configurations.
Transmission from assets to the rest of the system is represented using AC optimal power flow, is limited by PTDF and considers phase angles.
Available investment limits the total capacity of new assets that can be feasibly purchased.
Weather and market uncertainties are mitigated against using two-stage stochastic optimisation.
Externalities (loads, changes to asset capacities beyond the current portfolio) must be forecast over the next 10-15 years.

Profit-maximisation must be represented in how the portfolio is committed and dispatched in the day-ahead and intra-day markets, which requires competitors and their perceived risk appetite to be resolved.
